entry.title: Original King Crimson Drummer Michael Giles Dead At 84
entry.summary: Michael Giles, the original drummer of English prog-rock titans King Crimson, has died. Discipline Global Mobile, the record label founded by his old bandmate Robert Fripp, shared the news today, confirming that Giles passed away on Nov. 23. He was 84. Born in 1942, Giles got his start playing in bands with his bassist brother…
entry.content:
Michael Giles, the original drummer of English prog-rock titans King Crimson, has died. Discipline Global Mobile, the record label founded by his old bandmate Robert Fripp, shared the news today, confirming that Giles passed away on Nov. 23. He was 84.

Born in 1942, Giles got his start playing in bands with his bassist brother Peter. When they posted a newspaper advertisement looking for a keyboardist who could sing, they instead found Robert Fripp, a guitarist who couldn't. Nevertheless, they formed the trio of Giles, Giles & Fripp, signing to Deram and releasing a lone album, The Cheerful Insanity of Giles, Giles & Fripp, in 1968.

Following the addition of multi-instrumentalist Ian McDonald and the departure of Peter Giles, the group morphed into the first incarnation of King Crimson, rounded out by bassist/vocalist Greg Lake and lyricist Peter Sinfield. Michael Giles played on their landmark 1969 debut In The Court Of The Crimson King before leaving the band, although he still contributed to their 1970 follow-up In The Wake Of Poseidon.

Giles briefly formed a duo with fellow former King Crimson member Ian McDonald, releasing the self-titled album McDonald And Giles in 1970. He then transitioned into a successful career as a session musician, working with acts including Steve Winwood, Bryan Ferry, Leo Sayer, Anthony Phillips, Kevin Ayers, Greg Lake, Neil Sedaka, Yvonne Elliman, Rupert Hine, Roger Glover, Francis Monkman, Andy Summers, Peter Sinfield, and the Penguin Cafe Orchestra.

In 2001, Giles released his first solo album, Progress. A year later, he co-founded the 21st Century Schizoid Band, performing material from King Crimson's early period with other ex-members. He released his most recent solo album, Shadows/Solo, earlier this year.

entry.title: Rose Chamber Announce Debut Album My Silhouette: Hear “Modern Rot”
entry.summary: Ace Stallings is a familiar face on the national hardcore circuit. I know him a little bit — great guy. In addition to promoting shows and doing the interview podcast Forum Of Passion, Stallings has fronted a ton of bands: Break Away, Mutually Assured Destruction, Sentinel, Eliminators. In 2024, Stallings launched Rose Chamber, a project…
entry.content:
Ace Stallings is a familiar face on the national hardcore circuit. I know him a little bit — great guy. In addition to promoting shows and doing the interview podcast Forum Of Passion, Stallings has fronted a ton of bands: Break Away, Mutually Assured Destruction, Sentinel, Eliminators. In 2024, Stallings launched Rose Chamber, a project different from any he'd done before.

Rose Chamber, named after a great Mutually Assured Destruction song, is the duo of Stallings and Evan Schlomann, his bandmate in Sentinal. (Schlomann has also been in bands like Casket Architects and Night Terrors.) They make cold, mean, gothed-out synthpop, and Stallings' Danzig-esque bellow sounds really cool over that kind of music.

Rose Chamber already released the 2024 EP State Of Affairs and Double Feature, a 2025 split with the Shape. All of the tracks on those records will appear on Rose Chamber's full-length debut My Silhouette, along with new tracks like the awesomely mean opener "Modern Rot." As someone who writes a column about the Billboard Modern Rock chart, I appreciate that title. Check out the "Modern Rot" video below.

TRACKLIST:
01 "Modern Rot"
02 "It Only Gets Worse"
03 "No Sanctuary"
04 "I Am The Truth
05 "Beyond My Door"
06 "Intermezzo II"
07 "Immortal Tragedy"
08 "Past Sins"
09 "Intermezzo"
10 "State Of Affairs"
11 "At War"
12 "Ich Brauche"

My Silhouette is out 1/22 on Avant! Records.

entry.title: Anna Meredith – “Mink”
entry.summary: Listen to Scottish composer Anna Meredith's new song "Mink" from her upcoming studio album 'DARLING,' the follow-up to 2019's 'FIBS.'
entry.content:
Fresh off of her score for Wicker, the heavily memed film in which Academy Award winner Olivia Colman fucks a man made out of wicker played by Alexander Skarsgård, Scottish composer Anna Meredith is returning with her first official studio album since 2019's FIBS. DARLING will be out in February, and we've already heard its bright and frenetic opening track and lead single "Dusky." Follow-up "Mink" is calmer but no less imposing, a cresting wave of strings and synths. Meredith explains:

To me "Mink" is the "heart" of the album and a very different kind of intensity to lots of the other music. As with so much of the material, it’s the blend of the electronics and acoustic instruments that I hope gives it its sonic identity. In "Mink" the idea is a bending, pulsing core which is set within these massive synth chords right from the opening but this sinew-y pulsed idea grows and grows in power, infecting the rest of the instruments. The peak of the track grows to this exaggerated, intense almost strobe-like idea of what started as a smaller thread. We recorded this track with a string ensemble made from incredibly talented friends (and the best string players I know). I’m so grateful to them for such beautiful playing.

The track has a performance video from longtime collaborator Ewan Jones Morris filmed at Lightroom in King's Cross. Watch and listen below.

DARLING is out 2/12 via Mercury KX. Pre-order it here.

entry.title: Manchester Police Say Don Toliver Concert Gas Incident May Be Linked To Jewelry Thefts
entry.summary: On Sunday night, the newly dominant rap star Don Toliver performed for an audience of 12,000 at Manchester’s Co-op Live, but the show descended into chaos. Midway through Toliver’s performance, police evacuated the arena after people in the crowd breathed what cops describe as an “unknown substance,” widely believed to be tear gas. The show…
entry.content:
On Sunday night, the newly dominant rap star Don Toliver performed for an audience of 12,000 at Manchester's Co-op Live, but the show descended into chaos. Midway through Toliver's performance, police evacuated the arena after people in the crowd breathed what cops describe as an "unknown substance," widely believed to be tear gas. The show never restarted, and Toliver postponed two planned gigs at London's O2 Arena in the aftermath. Now, Manchester police claim that the tear-gassing incident could've been linked to a few jewelry robberies that reportedly took place during the show.

In a statement on their website yesterday, Manchester police said:

As part of progressing enquiries, detectives are exploring the possibility that release of the substance could be linked to reports of a small number of robbery offences at the arena on Sunday evening.

It comes after we received nine reports of jewellery being stolen during the same concert. No arrests have been made at this time.

As part of that statement, Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding says, "We are aware similar robberies have been reported at two European concerts for the same artist and will be linking in with our European counterparts to better understand the wider picture of this suspected offending."

Chain-snatchings at rap shows are nothing new, but apparently some thieves also use pepper spray or tear gas to set off panicked reactions in crowded spaces and make it easier to grab other people's stuff. After the 2017 terrorist attack that killed 22 people at an Ariana Grande show, arena concerts in Manchester must be awfully tense. I'm sure that makes it easier to start a panic, and that also makes it an even more despicable thing to do.

Yesterday, Co-op Live posted their own statement, saying that they've learned there's "no ongoing risk" from that evacuation and that all scheduled concerts at the venue will happen as planned.

On Monday, Toliver posted about the incident and his postponed London shows on his Instagram story, writing, "The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my Fans ! STOP BRING BULLSHIT INTO MY SHOWS!! it ain’t Cool see you soon London. Love you Guys."

entry.title: Vince Staples Covers A Geto Boys Classic In The BBC Live Lounge
entry.summary: You don’t see too many rappers doing cover songs. Rap is too subjective for that, too focused on projection of the self. Samples and quotes and allusions are one thing, but covers are another. Vince Staples doesn’t care. Staples covered the Geto Boys’ unimpeachable 1991 classic “Mind Playing Tricks On Me” on a recent visit…
entry.content:
You don't see too many rappers doing cover songs. Rap is too subjective for that, too focused on projection of the self. Samples and quotes and allusions are one thing, but covers are another. Vince Staples doesn't care. Staples covered the Geto Boys' unimpeachable 1991 classic "Mind Playing Tricks On Me" on a recent visit to the BBC Live Lounge, taking a deeply familiar track and putting a different spin on it. He made the song his own. That's what a cover is supposed to be.

Earlier this year, Staples released his Loma Vista debut Cry Baby, an album that gets into indie rock sonics without really altering Staples' point of view. He's touring with a live band. In his Live Lounge session, Staples and his band did the Cry Baby tracks "White Flag" and "Cotton." Then, they took on "Mind Playing Tricks On Me," a song that's two years older than Staples himself. For many of us, "Mind Playing Tricks" is the song we might find ourselves absentmindedly rapping word-for-word, getting to the Willie D verse before we even realize what we're doing. It's a bit like a folk song in that way.

For the Live Lounge performance, Staples' band worked up a supremely laid-back version of the "Mind Playing Tricks" beat. Staples rapped the whole song with reverence, though he took out all the cusswords for some reason. (Can you not cuss in the Live Lounge?) But where the Geto Boys hit every word with wild early-'90s levels of emphasis, Staples just kind of sleepily murmurs the verses. It sounds nice! Watch the full Live Lounge performance below.

Cry Baby is out now on Loma Vista.

entry.title: Watch Erykah Badu’s Weird, Great Fallon Performance
entry.summary: It took forever, but we finally got a new Erykah Badu album this year. Badu and the Alchemist joined forces to release the lovely, spaced-out, singular collaborative LP Before The World Blows, and if you’re looking for reasons to be thankful tomorrow, there’s one for you. One of the nice things about a new Erykah…
entry.content:
It took forever, but we finally got a new Erykah Badu album this year. Badu and the Alchemist joined forces to release the lovely, spaced-out, singular collaborative LP Before The World Blows, and if you're looking for reasons to be thankful tomorrow, there's one for you. One of the nice things about a new Erykah Badu album is that it put her back on TV, and that's what happened on Jimmy Fallon's Tonight Show on Tuesday.

As far as I can tell, Badu's appearance on last night's Fallon was her first time playing late-night TV in nearly nine years. She really made an event of it, too. Badu sang the Before The World Blows track "Breezy," an affectionate ode to a girl in a car, and she went all-out with her staging.

For nearly half of the song, last night's performance was a tight close-up on Badu in a blonde wig and a brown '70s-looking suit, holding a steering wheel and pretending to drive. The outfit might be a cinematic reference, but I'm not sure. Behind her, a screen made it look a bit like she was driving through a blurry cityscape, then floating in a pink bubble over a CGI skyline.

Halfway through, when the "Bennie And The Jets" sample came in, the screen dropped away and showed Badu's backing band, sans Alchemist. It's a little weird to see Badu playing Fallon without the Roots, her old comrades, but she and her band are all the way locked in right now. Watch the performance below.

Before The World Blows is out now on Control FREAQ Records/Young Recordings.

entry.title: Ninajirachi Shares I Love My Computer Remix Album Feat. Wet Leg, Slayr, Genesis Owusu, More
entry.summary: Last year, the Australian dance/hyperpop producer Ninajirachi released her utterly charming album I Love My Computer. It was one of our favorite records of 2025, and Ninajirachi was one of our favorite new artists. Since then, Ninajirachi has taken the fuck off, playing to big rooms and rapturous festival crowds. Along the way, she’s gotten…
entry.content:
Last year, the Australian dance/hyperpop producer Ninajirachi released her utterly charming album I Love My Computer. It was one of our favorite records of 2025, and Ninajirachi was one of our favorite new artists. Since then, Ninajirachi has taken the fuck off, playing to big rooms and rapturous festival crowds. Along the way, she's gotten to know a lot of her contemporaries. Today, she's back with a remix album called I Love My Computer, All My Friends Are Inside It.

There are 20 remixes on I Love My Computer, All My Friends Are Inside It, but not all of them are new. Since she put out the original I Love My Computer, Ninajirachi has dropped remixes from acts like Frost Children, underscores, Madeon, Effy, horsegiirL, and 100 gecs' Dylan Brady. I Love My Computer, All My Friends Are Inside It collects all those reworkings, as well as new ones from acts like Wet Leg, Slayr, Genesis Owusu, DJ_Dave, Nikki Nair, nate sib and kimj, and Mallrat. It's fun to hear those tracks explored from all those different angles. In a press release, Ninajirachi says:

Most of my time making music is spent alone, so hearing these songs reimagined by an amazing lineup of artists has been really inspiring and emotional. For an album that was written about experiences I’ve had all on my own, I Love My Computer has connected me to people all around the world more than anything else ever has. It is hard to be eloquent about the time I’ve had with it. It’s just so cool. Literally right now I’m in Mexico City, and I’ve met new people this week that I would’ve never met without music and the internet. There is no time I’d rather be alive than right now. I’m so grateful to the artists for bringing so much of themselves to every new version. Some are new friends, some I've known since I released my first song as Ninajirachi. We've played shows together and been in the studio together, but we all found each other's music on the computer first.

Listen to the remix album below.

I Love My Computer, All My Friends Are Inside It is out now on NLV.

entry.title: Helena Deland – “Whole Life”
entry.summary: A chilly, sleepy morning just before a major holiday is an ideal time to hear a new song from Helena Deland. (Deland is Canadian, so I guess it’s not the day before a major holiday for her, but nevermind.) Early next year, Deland will release Eternity Shrugs, the follow-up to her lovely 2023 album Goodnight…
entry.content:
A chilly, sleepy morning just before a major holiday is an ideal time to hear a new song from Helena Deland. (Deland is Canadian, so I guess it's not the day before a major holiday for her, but nevermind.) Early next year, Deland will release Eternity Shrugs, the follow-up to her lovely 2023 album Goodnight Summerland. We've already posted her songs "How Do You Like Me Now" and "Tip Of My Tongue," and she's got a new one out today.

Deland's latest single is a short, soft, comfy acoustic number called "Whole Life." It's all about finding meaning when you meet someone else and maybe accepting that that's a temporary thing. In a press release, Deland says, "It’s hard to tell, from within something, what it will come to mean in the scope of one’s whole life. The song is about wanting to take in something that is bound to be short-lived. It weighs the denial and magical thinking required to keep a fragile thing going, and lives in the space between ‘Tell me’ and ‘Don’t tell me now,’ wanting to know, knowing already." Listen below.

Eternity Shrugs is out 1/22 on Chivi Chivi.

entry.title: Advance Base – “The 1st Noelle”
entry.summary: If I were to present you with the phrase, “Advance Base Christmas song,” what ideas would enter your brain? Would you mentally prepare yourself? Would you mentally prepare yourself enough? I hope you would. An Advance Base song can take place on the most beautiful spring day and still be the most depressing but somehow…
entry.content:
If I were to present you with the phrase, "Advance Base Christmas song," what ideas would enter your brain? Would you mentally prepare yourself? Would you mentally prepare yourself enough? I hope you would. An Advance Base song can take place on the most beautiful spring day and still be the most depressing but somehow also bleakly funny thing you'll hear all week. An Advance Base Christmas song? You're in for an experience.

If you're unfamiliar with Advance Base, it's Owen Ashworth, the dour-voiced singer-songwriter who once recorded as Casiotone For The Painfully Alone. He sings about dark circumstances with detached panache, and he conjures entire worlds of hurt in a few surgical words. Ashworth released Horrible Occurrences, his most recent Advance Base album, at the tail-end of 2024, and he came out with a two-song single last year. Today, he's got a new song about a very rough holiday.

"The 1st Noelle" is set to the tune of "The First Noel," a song that you absolutely know, but it's sung from the perspective of someone who's basically homeless on Christmas after breaking up with a girl named Noelle. As in: "'The 1st, Noelle,' the new landlord did say/ 'You can come get the keys on New Year's Day.'" The whole story unfolds over two minutes, and I like where it ends up.

"The 1st Noelle" has some backup vocals from Moontype’s Margaret McCarthy, who also sang backup on "Movie Theater Manager," one of the tracks that Advance Base released last year. A few months ago, Advance Base and Moontype also released the collaborative live album In Milwaukee. Listen to "The 1st Noelle" below.

entry.title: Hell Hath No Fury Turns 20
entry.summary: The labels weren’t playing fair jive. That was the narrative. Everybody else was getting richer than Scrooge McDuck, but the Thornton brothers, Malice and Pusha T, were stuck on the shelf, casualties of a corporate restructuring that they were too disgusted to navigate. Somehow, some way, the Clipse had made it out of Virginia Beach…
entry.content:
• Re-Up Gang/Star Trak/Arista/Zomba
  • 2006

The labels weren't playing fair jive. That was the narrative. Everybody else was getting richer than Scrooge McDuck, but the Thornton brothers, Malice and Pusha T, were stuck on the shelf, casualties of a corporate restructuring that they were too disgusted to navigate. Somehow, some way, the Clipse had made it out of Virginia Beach and started making hits. Thanks in large part to the Neptunes, the suddenly hot production duo who put them on and produced their entire debut album, Clipse had taken their dead-eyed and densely constructed tales of dirty money straight to the radio. Then one company bought another company, and the brothers got shuffled off to some label that hadn't signed them and sued to get out of their deal. It took them more than four years, an eternity in rap time, to follow up their gold-selling 2002 album Lord Willin'. Their momentum was lost, and they were pissed the fuck off.

With two decades of distance, we can now say that the clueless corporate label people did all of us a favor. By wasting all that momentum and alienating the brothers, those business idiots gave the Clipse enough venom to motivate them to record some of the sharpest, meanest rap music in history. In destroying any chance that the Clipse might make another radio hit on the level of "Grindin'," the already-unconventional thwack-snarl that the duo rode to success, they allowed the Thorntons to realize that they needn't bother even trying to make something that might cross over. Instead, label negligence gave the duo permission to make a sonically hostile art-rap tour de force that pushed their confrontational sound and appeal to its logical extreme, leaving us with a diamond-hard masterpiece that sounds as good today as it did when it came out, exactly two decades ago come Saturday. Clipse are legends today because the labels fucked them up.

Clipse had done this dance before. In 1999, as the Neptunes were just starting to build a catalog, they helped broker a deal between Clipse and Elektra, but the duo's would-be debut album Exclusive Audio Footage never came out. With Lord Willin', they got another shot, and they connected. The Neptunes produced the whole record, and their oblique funk worked just right with the Clipse's nihilistically frank trafficking talk. For a minute, Clipse were in radio rotation alongside Nelly and Ludacris. They made "What Happened To That Boy" with Birdman, and that experience apparently led to a rift with Cash Money that would continue to reverberate for decades. But when label reshuffling moved the Clipse from Arista to Jive, not even their connection to the peak-era Neptunes could save the Clipse. They had blown up with "Grindin'," but they found themselves back on the shelf, with no option but to grind.

They did something about it. They sued to get out of their contract, which probably took them out of the game for even longer, and they let their frustration out on their classic We Got It 4 Cheap mixtapes. There, they sneered at the suits and vowed to keep their alternate income streams flowing if the recording contracts didn't line up right: "Fuck Zomba, I sell nose candy, Willy Wonka." What they didn't expect was that those two Got It 4 Cheap mixtapes, especially 2005's exceptional Vol. 2, would find them a whole new audience of critics and hipsters. Suddenly, the Clipse were cool, a state of being that they'd never bothered to chase. Maybe that emboldened them, or maybe they already knew they were the shit. Either way, the newfound love didn't hurt.

Finally, lawsuits were settled, deals signed, and the prospect of a second Clipse album became real. The release of Hell Hath No Fury was endlessly delayed, but it finally arrived in stores on the Tuesday after Thanksgiving, sending critics scrambling to reorder their year-end lists. Clipse, scarred and angry over those contract battles, opted not to even try to generate income for the labels that had forsaken them. Instead, they resolved to make the malevolent masterwork that they knew they had in them. They attacked the task with purpose. There would be no hits, no superstar crossovers. There would only be vengeance.

Hell Hath No Fury is not a record made in conversation with the rest the rap music of its day. Lord Willin' is a hard, rigorous album in its own right, but it has frothy party songs and hooky for-the-ladies songs. B-list stars like Fabolous and Jermaine Dupri make appearances. It's an album made with commercial considerations in mind. Even if Clipse didn't expect it to be a blockbuster, they probably knew they could parlay its success into, say, appearing on Justin Timberlake's first solo single. On Hell Hath No Fury, that's all gone. Clipse's only collaborators are the close friends who were on the same wavelength and, for one hook, their fellow Neptunes beneficiary Slim Thug, whose own spotlight moment was right about to end.

Hell Hath No Fury doesn't sound like a major-label rap record from 2006. It doesn't sound like snap music or hyphy or triumphantly larger-than-life Atlanta trap à la T.I. or Young Jeezy, nor does it sound like a reaction against those things. It doesn't sound like an indie-label rap record from 2006, either. For that matter, it doesn't sound like a major or indie rap record from any other year. Instead, it sounds like Clipse and their small circle of collaborators closing ranks and speaking to each other. It's sui generis — influenced, more than anything, by itself.

When Clipse made the We Got It 4 Cheap mixtapes, they hijacked the hottest beats of the moment and used them for their own purposes — the same strategy that turned their adversary Lil Wayne into rap's biggest star during that same moment. But Clipse weren't trying to become Wayne. They only wanted to post up on the sidelines, staring at Wayne with abject disgust. That's what lead single "Mr. Me Too" is about.

The real issues between Wayne and Clipse were a lot deeper than the fact that Wayne started wearing Bathing Ape after Clipse did. That's just a stand-in for some larger gripes, like the fact that suddenly every big rap star spent all their time discussing the intricacies of the cocaine trade. Even if its focus is small, "Mr. Me Too" still sounds gigantic. Intentionally or not, Pharrell's verse plays as a grim parody of cash-money millionaire excess: "Just last week, I was out in Aspen/ Me and Puff hoppin' off a plane, both us laughin'." But Malice and Pusha T aren't up in Donatella's crib with 10 hoes. They've got other concerns, like the dumb shit that their peers were doing in their absence: "I was just assumin' you'd keep the coke movin'/ But I got one question: Fuck y'all been doin'?"

Pusha T hits that fuck so hard. He and Malice hit everything so hard, intoning phrases that continue to ricochet around inside my skull. "Have that money right or end up in the truck taped up." "Peel money rolls till our thumbs get the papercuts." "Who gon' stop us? Not a got-damn one of ya." They reel off designer names with joyless precision, like they're annoyed that they have to tell you these things that you should already know. Meanwhile, the Neptunes beats — just Pharrell operating independently of his onetime partner Chad Hugo, according to Clipse interviews from years later — make up a dumbfounding tapestry of drones and hums and subsonic rumbles, pierced by militant handclaps, mechanized ratatat snare-bursts, and syncopated shakers. This was what they sent to radio.

"Wamp Wamp," the second single, wasn't much friendlier. At least theoretically, a catchphrase-driven Slim Thug hook might've been enough to convince some skeptics in the aftermath of Houston screw's big pop moment. But the frantically ping-ponging steel drums and bagpipes ensured that wasn't going to happen. "Wamp Wamp" sounds less like Houston, more like the Hadron Collider. The drums are all upside down, and Pusha T's skip-scatter verse is all big-money word games: "Can't stand the bright from the ice, the chain xenon lamp ya." You have to feel for the girls who had to figure out how to shake ass to that all-elbows music in the video.

All of Hell Hath No Fury sits in that register. The Neptunes were able to make brain-scattering pop hits out of discordant keyboard-blats and empty space, but the Hell Hath No Fury production turns their sound into funky abstraction. Nothing makes sense — the stuttering harp-string sustain of "Ride Around Shining," the gasping choirs and swimming-upstream woodblocks of "Keys Open Doors," the wildly panning hovering-spaceship vwerps of "Trill." Even at their most outlandish, though, those tracks always hit with the brisk simplicity of a Marley Marl track. Malice and Pusha T always found the pockets on those beats. They rapped over berserk sounds like it was a normal thing to do.

There are a few slight tonal shifts on Hell Hath No Fury, as on the regretful and downbeat ballad "Nightmares." But in a time of jagged, piecemeal multi-producer rap records, Clipse simply continued to chip away at the same piece of marble. Hell Hath No Fury is a tight, focused record. The mood remains consistent throughout. Even when Clipse talk to the ladies on "Dirty Money," they're making a point, not flirting. The album never ventures far from the heightened realm of the coke-dealer lifestyle. So even when Clipse tell you about all the baubles they'll buy for you, they make sure you know that they're buying those baubles with ill-gotten gains. "Now, tell me: Is the dirty money really that bad?" — the question is rhetorical.

Two years after the release of Hell Hath No Fury, Malice rapped, "I'm not a part of your coke-rap genre." This was a clear message to the many, many critics, me probably included, who fixated on all of the album's artfully brusque yayo talk: "Open the Frigidaire, 25 to life in there/ So much white you might think your holy Christ was near," "Coke money clean through Merrill Lynch, accountant just gasp at the smell of it." And it's true that Clipse didn't talk about selling coke the same way that contemporaries like Jeezy and Cam'ron did. Instead, it's a crucial part of a larger backdrop.

The criminal underworld of Hell Hath No Fury isn't compelling just because they're talking about cocaine. It's compelling because it's about life lived at extremes, which allows them to get into paranoia, distrust, jealousy, bulletproof confidence, moneyed instability, and all sorts of other ideas. I'm writing this while fully immersed in Grand Theft Auto VI, the biggest sensation in any medium this year, and it's set in the exact same world. There's a reason that Miami Vice lifestyle fascinates even those of us who never touch cocaine crumbs, either as sellers or buyers.

When Hell Hath No Fury arrived, what really stood out was the imperious wordplay, the way that the Clipse bent language into dazzling new shapes without ever veering into abstraction: "Flow chameleon, worth 'bout a million/ Sell Bolivian, feds in oblivion/ Bitch Brazilian, purse reptilian/ Took her from far-off island like Gilligan." Listening to it today, that stuff remains astonishing, but now it's enriched by the past two decades of Clipse history — their long hiatus, Pusha's solo run, Malice's religious awakening, their eventual triumphant return.

Almost every track on Hell Hath No Fury follows the same blueprint: Pusha verse, hook, Malice verse, hook, back-and-forth Pusha-and-Malice verse, final hook, moment for the beat to ride out. If there's a guest, they'll mix the formula up slightly, but it'll almost always be Pusha first, then Malice. The construction throws their personality differences into relief. Pusha is flashier, angrier, and more militant: "They're prayin' I never go solo." Malice's heavy conscience and inner-conflict torment, always present in the music, become louder. Back then, I took "Momma I'm So Sorry" as facetious shit-talk. Listening now, it sounds a lot more like an actual sincere apology. Malice still talks his shit, but he clearly hates to think that his little brother ever had to get involved in a fundamentally amoral life.

When Hell Hath No Fury finally came out, the Clipse were subject to a whole lot of pocket-watching. This was a time when, at least in rap, record sales were all bound up with cultural influence and artistic respect. An album that didn't move Kanye West numbers could become an object of ridicule on the XXL blogs. Hell Hath No Fury got rapturous reviews, including a rare XXL rating from XXL itself, but maybe that only meant that critics were hopelessly out of touch with rap's audience. In any case, Hell Hath No Fury, an album that was never intended to become a blockbuster, did not become a blockbuster. Instead, it debuted at #14 and never even went gold. In some people's eyes, it was a failure. But it mattered.

Today, Hell Hath No Fury stands as an early example of major-label prestige-rap. It's somewhere between mainstream and underground, and it resonated in ways that the charts could never properly convey. The critical acclaim made a reputational difference, if not a commercial one. On the 2006 Pazz & Jop poll, Hell Hath No Fury finished at #7, between the Arctic Monkeys and Neko Case. Now that I look at that list, some of the other rap records in the top 40 — Ghostface Killah's Fishscale, the Roots' Game Theory, Lupe Fiasco's Food & Liquor — fit somewhere into that prestige-rap dynamic, too. (T.I.'s King, J Dilla's Donuts, and the Coup's Pick A Bigger Weapon are on there, as well, but it's a lot easier to place those records on the mainstream/underground divide.)

Clipse discovered that they had a very real audience, though it probably wasn't the one that they wanted. They embraced the new crowd, to an extent. They played indie rock festivals like Pitchfork as well as big rap shows like the Brooklyn one I went to that was supposed to celebrate the launch of the Zune. They opened for Modest Mouse. These days, Clipse are once again fixtures on the music-festival landscape. But after Hell Hath No Fury, they tried to swing back toward rap's mainstream. Their 2009 follow-up Till The Casket Drops had boldfaced-name guests — Kanye West, Cam'ron — and production from people other than the Neptunes. It was not the same uncompromising object as Hell Hath No Fury, and it didn't have the same impact. Soon after its release, Malice decided that he was done, and Pusha became the sharpest shooter on West's G.O.O.D. Music roster.

Nineteen years after Hell Hath No Fury, Clipse finally returned with Let God Sort Em Out, and they sounded more rejuvenated than anyone could've hoped. They explicitly made that record in the image of Hell Hath No Fury, holing up with Pharrell and shutting out all possible contemporary influences. It's a distant echo, but it was strong enough to finally earn the Clipse respect from institutions — the Grammys, the Vatican — that ignored Hell Hath No Fury. Once again, they had to go through a whole lot of label bullshit to release the album that they wanted to release. Once again, the label idiots might've done us a favor.

Clipse - Hell Hath No Fury [Gold Vinyl]

entry.title: Seal Returns The Honor And Covers Tame Impala
entry.summary: Last month, for Australian radio station Triple J’s covers series Like A Version, national hero Tame Impala opted to perform Seal’s haunting ’90s hit “Kiss From A Rose.” Kevin Parker said he and his bandmates initially balked at attempting the “quite proggy” ballad, but once they accepted that none of them could sing it like…
entry.content:
Last month, for Australian radio station Triple J's covers series Like A Version, national hero Tame Impala opted to perform Seal's haunting '90s hit "Kiss From A Rose." Kevin Parker said he and his bandmates initially balked at attempting the "quite proggy" ballad, but once they accepted that none of them could sing it like Seal, they were content to let their Aussie bloke voices cascade as best they could.

Now Seal has returned the favor by covering "New Person, Same Old Mistakes," the closing track from Tame Impala's 2015 classic Currents. You know, the one Rihanna later sang over. "Felt a bit rude not to return the honor," Seal wrote in a social media post teasing the cover.

Seal recorded the cover at Dragonfly Creek Studios in Malibu with an acoustic ensemble including Simon Bloor on keys, Drew McKeon on percussion, Elise Trouw on bass, and Zach Wish on guitar. His voice remains incredible. Watch below.

entry.summary: The veteran experimental musician Rafael Toral has been on a dazzling run since returning to the guitar in recent years. It’s some of the most beautiful music I’ve ever heard, and he’s about to…
entry.content:
The veteran experimental musician Rafael Toral has been on a dazzling run since returning to the guitar in recent years. On his albums Spectral Evolution and Traveling Light, Toral has melted 20th-century jazz and pop standards into gorgeous ambient guitar drone. It's some of the most beautiful music I've ever heard, and he's about to unveil its next iteration.

In February, Toral will put out Long Ways, his latest release for Drag City. The album pares back the orchestral arrangements and celestial qualities of his recent work in favor of sparse, unvarnished guitar. This statement explains the approach, which seems to emphasize the silence around the notes as much as the music itself:

Long Ways is a development forward from the previous two albums, but condensing everything into playing guitar. It’s all about sound, or better, the stillness of presence. The music itself here is less important than the sound of playing. What I’m after is an abstraction, the sound of music.

I also like the way he describes his goals in a note to his Bandcamp followers: "Not really playing a sound, but the sound of playing. Not really music, but the sound of music." Below, get a glimpse of what he's aiming for in an excerpt released today titled "Long Ways Short 4."

02/13 - Antwerp, BE @ De Singel

entry.content:
Jorg Kuning: A name that I will never, ever learn to pronounce correctly. I might never even learn to pronounce it incorrectly. I could hurt myself trying. Even attempting to sound it out in my head without saying anything out loud, my brain only coughs up a series of Swedish Chef noises. And Jorg Kuning isn't even Swedish! He's Welsh! I have been to Wales, but that experience did not prepare me to deal with Jorg Kuning's name.

Jorg Kuning is the adventurous dance DJ and producer who released the EP Elvers Pass last year. His track "Synthetic Squashies" came in at #1 in our monthly dance roundup. Next year, Kuning will follow Elvers Pass with his full-length debut Clun Pearls. Its lead single is called "Bitzer's Cello," and I'm pretty sure I do hear some cello in with all the playful dance track's dizzily ping-ponging keyboard sounds. Check it out below.

entry.content:
Two compound words, one headline. I like it. We should keep smushing words together forever. We should do the whole headline as just one word. Punchbagfangirl. Would that be anything? Would Stereogum's beloved readership think the entire website had a stroke? Where would we put the quotation marks? Who cares! Rules don't matter! Everything is made-up! Punchbag! Fangirl!

Punchbag are not made-up. They're the London electro-pop duo of siblings Clara and Anders Bach, and their EP I Am Obsessed came out earlier this year. Their father Johann Sebastian Bach [citation needed] must be so proud. Today, they release a big, stomping headrush singalong called "Fangirl." It makes me think of Republica's "Ready To Go," which means I like it.

In a press release, Clara says, "Sometimes you write songs about the profound meaning of life and the dark interiors of your mental landscapes, and other times you write songs about going to a gig and having a massive crush on the girl with the guitar, and you know what, both are equally important." Counterpoint: the second one is way more important. Check out the "Fangirl" video below.

"Fangirl" is out now on Mute.

entry.content:
Beyond the obvious importance of the sound that they basically introduced, the Ramones were a fascinating band who left behind countless bangers even though they all hated each other. Next month, Stereogum will team up with LA's Sid The Cat Auditorium for a mini tribute show called Ramones Night.

Ramones Night goes down Dec. 7 at Sid The Cat Auditorium, and it includes a screening of Jim Fields and Michael Gramaglia's 2003 documentary End Of The Century: The Story Of The Ramones. That's one of the all-time great rock docs, and it's got heavier poignancy today because so many of its interview subjects, including all four original Ramones, are no longer with us.

Magnolia Pictures has a new 4K restoration of End Of The Century coming to theaters Dec. 11, and its first public screening is happening at Ramones Night. The evening starts with a 7 p.m. screening, with a Ramones tribute set with special guests happening afterward. Those guests will be announced later. Get your tickets here.

entry.summary: Last year, the swaggering Brighton duo Lambrini Girls earned a lot of attention for their debut album Who Let The Dogs Out, and they’ve earned praise from elder figures like Iggy Pop, Kathleen Hanna, and U2. Earlier this month, the Edge shouted them out, “I’m just so jealous of them. Now that’s a sound I…
entry.content:
Last year, the swaggering Brighton duo Lambrini Girls earned a lot of attention for their debut album Who Let The Dogs Out, and they've earned praise from elder figures like Iggy Pop, Kathleen Hanna, and U2. Earlier this month, the Edge shouted them out, "I’m just so jealous of them. Now that’s a sound I would love to hear on a U2 album. Just the sonics are fantastic." Sonically or otherwise, however, it's difficult to imagine U2 releasing a track anything like "Don't Talk To Me Until I've Had My Abortion."

Lambrini Girls' sophomore album No Refunds comes out in January, and they've already shared a handful of singles. Their latest is "Don't Talk To Me Until I've Had My Abortion." It's a snarling, sarcastic attack on the Biblical reasons that people devise to limit women's abortion rights: "If I’m a no good killer sinner whore/ Then don’t talk to me until I’ve had my abortion/ My body? Bullshit/ It never was." Listen below.

No Refunds is out 1/15 on City Slang. In conjunction with the new single, Lambrini Girls are launching a new fundraiser with ARC Southeast, an American organization that supports people who need abortion care.

(“Comet,” the Peel Dream Magazine collab that Joy shared in September, isn’t on the LP.) Today, Joy teams up with another dreamy indie auteur, Midwife’s Madeline Johnston, on the…
entry.content:
The Chicago musician Mia Joy will soon return with her long-awaited new album Star Echo Heavy Dove, and we posted lead single "Wings Of Desire" already. ("Comet," the Peel Dream Magazine collab that Joy shared in September, isn't on the LP.) Today, Joy teams up with another dreamy indie auteur, Midwife's Madeline Johnston, on the new track "Circle."

Mia Joy and Midwife have known one another for a long time, and their approaches really align on "Circle." It's a blissed-out sigh of a track. In a press release, Joy says that she and Midwife first played on the same bill in Chicago in 2018: "Like Author, Like Daughter saved my life. It was one of those moments where you hear something and you’re a fan for life... [Star Echo Heavy Dove] didn’t feel right not having Madeline on it. I just said ‘please,’ and she said ‘duh,’ and we did it." Here's what Johnston says about the collaboration:

I've been a fan of Mia since we played in Chicago together nearly 10 years ago now. It's been a pleasure to watch her project transform and grow over the years. Mia Joy's new album harnesses the softness and mysticism of Spirit Tamer with a new experimental edge. I'm so honored to play on 'Circle' and collaborate with another MJ!

Check out Cory Feder's animated "Circle" video below.

Star Echo Heavy Dove is out 1/15/27 on Fire Talk.

entry.title: Peter Gabriel – “Yes, It Will Go”
entry.summary: Art-rock eminence Peter Gabriel is nearly finished with the year-long rollout of his new album i/o. Gabriel has been releasing the album one track at a time, with new singles arriving with every new moon. Last month, for instance, he shared his song “Who Are We Talking To?” Technically, the full LP comes out on…
entry.content:
Art-rock eminence Peter Gabriel is nearly finished with the year-long rollout of his new album i/o. Gabriel has been releasing the album one track at a time, with new singles arriving with every new moon. Last month, for instance, he shared his song "Who Are We Talking To?" Technically, the full LP comes out on Friday. For now, Gabriel has shared penultimate track "Yes, It Will Go," a bittersweet piano-ballad about how nothing can ever last.

Gabriel wrote and produced "Yes, It Will Go" himself, and it's a soft, pretty reckoning. When you get older, you have to make peace with the idea that you're not going to last forever, and "Yes, It Will Go" sounds like Gabriel doing that in real time: "Everything's going to fade in time, just like the fallen snow/ And all the things that look so permanent will go." He is 76 years old, and there's something sad but comforting in hearing a man of his age and stature accepting the inevitable. Here's what Gabriel says about the track:

If you look at the chronological history of the development of all the songs, this was probably the newest, but it was one of the most emotional, so I am quite close to it. I've got some lovely singing from my daughter Melanie on the end of it, and it's a personal song for me.

I was trying to convey a sense that everything is in flux, it's all changing and the things that look permanent won't be. In addition, everything is also being accelerated with AI — along with the changes from climate change. There are all sorts of fundamental transitions that are happening so fast to us, and we need to be able to make ourselves more flexible and plastic to respond to them. It's going to be more and more important personally and as a society that we can accept that we're in a rapidly changing environment and adapt and plan for it, as much as we can.

As with all the i/o tracks, Gabriel has paired "Yes, It Will Go" with a piece of artwork. In this case, it's "Soul City (Pyramid Of Oranges)," a 1967 piece from the South African artist Roelof Louw. Here's what Gabriel says about it:

The image this month is something that I think articulates the theme of the song better than the song in a way. When I first saw it and I was looking for things that might represent impermanence, it was "bingo!" — this is what we have to use.

In a sense, there are two forces at work; there's the pyramid which for most of us is a symbol of permanence, but it's made up of oranges which we know will rot in the week. Of all the images on the record, this one, I think, was right on the spot. Other images we have create mood or encompass some of what the songs are trying to say, but this one hundred percent nailed it.

Below, check out "Yes, It Will Go" and a video of Gabriel recording the song and talking about it.

i/o is out 11/27 on Gabriel's own Real World label.
